- adaptive: Instructions to make or update an app's UI so that it adapts to different Android devices including phones, tablets, foldables, laptops, desktop, TV, Auto and XR. It includes how to handle different window sizes, pointing devices (such as mouse) and text entry devices (such as keyboard) using the Compose MediaQuery API. It also covers multi-pane layouts using Navigation3 Scenes, adaptive UI components (such as buttons) with varying target sizes, and adaptive layouts (including navigation areas - nav rails and nav bars) using the Compose Grid and FlexBox APIs.
- agp-9-upgrade: Upgrades, or migrates, an Android project to use Android Gradle Plugin (AGP) version 9. Do not use this skill for migrating Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) projects.
- android-cli: Provides instructions for installing and using the `android` CLI. The `android` command-line tool is a critical tool for Android development and helps you create new Android projects, run Android apps on devices, manage and interact with Android virtual devices (including screenshots and UI inspection), manage Android SDK components, look up official Android documentation, and discover and install official Android skills.
- android-intent-security: Best practices for Android Intent security. Use this skill when auditing component configurations in AndroidManifest.xml activities, services, receivers) or source code handling incoming Intents (getIntent, getParcelableExtra) to prevent Intent Redirection and unauthorized access.
- appfunctions: Analyzes Android apps to identify key user workflows for AppFunctions such as creating a note, playing media, or sending an automated or AI agent triggered message, voice commands, or system shortcuts, without needing to open the app UI. Generates Kotlin code to expose these workflows to the Android system, allowing agents to discover and execute them on-device. Also refines KDoc documentation to ensure AI agents correctly understand and use the provided functionality.
- camerax: Provide technical guidance for Android camera development with CameraX. Use when implementing camera features, handling asynchronous recording lifecycles, wiring low-level hardware interop using CameraX, or integrating ML Kit or Media3 effects.
- display-glasses-with-jetpack-compose-glimmer: Provides guidelines for developing projected Android XR apps for display glasses using the Jetpack Compose Glimmer UI toolkit. This skill covers foundational Glimmer design principles, workflows for implementing Jetpack Compose Glimmer, and interaction models for the glasses form factor. Use this skill to build an Android XR Augmented Experience app with Jetpack Compose Glimmer that adheres to the Glimmer design system for optimized glasses styling.
- edge-to-edge: Use this skill to migrate your Jetpack Compose app to add adaptive edge-to-edge support and troubleshoot common issues. Use this skill to fix UI components (like buttons or lists) that are obscured by or overlapping with the navigation bar or status bar, fix IME insets, and fix system bar legibility.
- engage-sdk-integration: Helps developers integrate, debug, and resolve Play Engage SDK implementation issues. Use when adding Engage SDK support, generating publishing code, mapping data classes to entities, or fixing SDK-related errors.
- migrate-xml-views-to-jetpack-compose: Provides a structured workflow for migrating an Android XML View to Jetpack Compose. This skill details the step-by-step process, from planning and dependency setup, to theming and layout migration, validation and XML cleanup. Use this skill when you need to migrate an XML View to Jetpack Compose in an Android project. It solves the problem of converting the UI of a legacy XML View into modern, declarative Compose components while maintaining interoperability.
- navigation-3: Learn how to install and migrate to Jetpack Navigation 3, and how to implement features and patterns such as deep links, multiple backstacks, scenes (dialogs, bottom sheets, list-detail, two-pane, supporting pane), conditional navigation (such as logged-in navigation versus anonymous), returning results from flows, integration with Hilt, ViewModel, Kotlin, and view interoperability.
- perfetto-sql: Translates natural language data intents into syntactically valid Perfetto SQL queries and executes them against a local trace file. Use this skill to extract slice, thread, or memory data from Android Perfetto traces using trace_processor.
- perfetto-trace-analysis: Analyzes Perfetto traces to find the root cause of latency, memory, or jank issues in Android apps. Use when the user provides a Perfetto trace file and asks any question, ongoing investigation, or open-ended request to analyze its contents.
- play-billing-library-version-upgrade: Use this skill when upgrading or migrating an Android project from any legacy Google Play Billing Library (PBL) version to the latest stable version of PBL.
- r8-analyzer: Analyzes Android build files and R8 keep rules to identify redundancies, broad package-wide rules, and rules that subsume library consumer keep rules. Use when developers want to optimize their app's size, remove redundant or overly broad keep rules, or troubleshoot Proguard configurations.
- styles: Use this skill to integrate the Jetpack Compose Styles API into an Android project. This skill guides you through upgrading dependencies, setting up component themes, making custom components styleable, and migrating existing layout properties to use unified styles. Migrate custom design system components, replace hard coded parameters with Style attributes, and use Modifier.styleable for interaction states.
- testing-setup: Analyze and create a testing strategy for native Android apps - install testing libraries, set up test infrastructure, create harnesses for unit tests, UI tests, screenshot tests, and end-to-end tests.
- verified-email: Provides a complete workflow for implementing verified email retrieval on Android Credential Manager API. Use this skill to integrate a secure, OTP-less email verification flow into an Android app. This skill solves the problem of high-friction sign-up processes by leveraging cryptographically verified credentials from trusted providers like Google.
- wear-compose-m3: Expert guidance for working with Wear OS Compose Material3. Use this skill when creating, updating, or migrating Wear OS projects. This includes the androidx.wear.compose.material3, androidx.wear.compose.foundation, and androidx.wear.compose.navigation3 libraries. Also working with core components such as AppScaffold, ScreenScaffold, and TransformingLazyColumn, and core Wear OS concepts such as ambient mode. Migration from lower versions such as Material 2.5 and Horologist.
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- core:architecture-ports: Apply ports & adapters (hexagonal) and clean-architecture rules when designing or reviewing how modules depend on each other — the dependency rule (domain imports no framework), repositories that hide storage, constructor dependency injection, structural interfaces/Protocols over inheritance, single-responsibility services, and DTOs across boundaries instead of ORM rows. Use when adding a service, repository, adapter, port, or handler; when wiring dependencies; when a domain module starts importing a framework/ORM/HTTP/cloud SDK; or when a file mixes business logic with I/O. Do NOT use for pure language-syntax style (types, formatting), test authoring, or security/authz review — those have their own skills.
- core:documentation: Guidance for writing and maintaining project documentation that stays accurate — keep one source of truth and link instead of duplicating, update docs in the same change as the code they describe, co-locate context with the code it explains, maintain a code-to-docs mapping so changes know which doc to touch, and never leave scratch files. Use when adding or editing README/architecture/integration docs, deciding where a piece of documentation belongs, reviewing a PR that changes behavior but not docs, or cleaning up stray notes/TODO files. Do NOT use for API reference auto-generated from code comments, or for code-style/testing rules.
- core:fail-fast: Apply fail-fast error handling — raise immediately on missing or invalid required values instead of returning null/defaults, never swallow exceptions in empty catch blocks, and use typed/custom error classes with actionable context. Use this skill when writing or reviewing error handling, validation, config/parameter reading, try/catch or try/except blocks, or when a defect surfaces far from its cause (works then breaks weirdly later). Trigger keywords — silent fallback, default value, swallowed exception, empty catch, error handling, defensive coding, guard clause. Do NOT use this skill for designing immutable data models (use immutability) or for forward-compatible unused parameters (use forward-compat-slots).
- core:forward-compat-slots: Apply the forward-compatible reserved-injection-slot convention — a constructor or function parameter prefixed with underscore AND typed optional is an intentionally-unused dependency slot kept so future callers can inject it without touching every call site. Use this skill when adding a dependency to a base class or shared signature that not all implementations use yet, when a composing facade must pass the same dependency uniformly to sub-services, when reviewing an unused parameter, or when deciding whether to delete vs keep an unused argument. Trigger keywords — unused parameter, reserved slot, forward compatibility, optional dependency, _logger, _param, injection slot. Do NOT use this skill for general immutability (use immutability) or fail-fast error handling (use fail-fast).
- core:immutability: Minimize mutability — default domain types to immutable, derive new state with copy-on-write instead of mutating in place, never mutate function arguments, and keep a pure functional core with side effects pushed to a thin imperative shell. Use this skill when designing data models, value objects, or state-transition logic; when reviewing code that mutates shared state, reassigns variables, or mutates passed-in arguments; or when separating business logic from I/O. Trigger keywords — mutable state, in-place mutation, copy-on-write, immutable, frozen, readonly, value object, functional core, shared state bug. Do NOT use this skill for error-handling/fallback decisions (use fail-fast) or for reserved unused parameters (use forward-compat-slots).
- core:pr-authoring: Apply evidence-based pull-request authoring practice — keep each change small (~100-300 lines of substantive change) and single-concern, link the issue so your tracker auto-updates, and follow your team's chosen PR workflow and merge style well. This skill presents the trade-offs of mono-PR vs stacked PRs and squash vs merge-commit rather than mandating one (record your team's pick in .claude/rules/team-conventions.md). Use this skill when opening a PR, sizing or splitting a change, naming a branch, writing a PR description, or deciding mono vs stacked. Trigger keywords — open a PR, pull request, branch name, PR description, split this change, change size, mono PR, stacked PR, squash, merge strategy, rebase. Do NOT use this skill for reviewing someone else's PR (use pr-review) or for commit-message wording alone.
- core:pr-review: Apply evidence-based code-review practice when reviewing a pull request or diff — calibrate review depth to the change's risk and blast radius, raise one finding per concern, classify each on a Required/Nit/Question severity ladder, and shape each comment as problem-grounded-in-the-diff then why-it-matters then a concrete fix. Use this skill when reviewing a PR, reading a diff, writing review comments, deciding review depth, triaging which findings block merge, or dispatching per-concern review passes. Trigger keywords — review this PR, code review, review the diff, review comment, severity, required vs nit, blocking finding, reviewer. Do NOT use this skill for authoring/sizing your own PR (use pr-authoring) or for running a specific language's linter/typechecker.
- core:secure-coding: Apply OWASP-based secure-coding rules when writing or reviewing code that handles authorization, secrets, logging, external input, persistence, network calls, or mobile local storage — server-side deny-by-default authz on every object/property/function, no hardcoded secrets (centralized store + rotation), never logging secrets/tokens/PII, validate-and-encode all external input, and mobile OS key stores with no plaintext local storage and TLS. Use when adding an endpoint/handler, an auth or ownership check, a logging statement, a DB or shell query, a config/secret read, an IAM policy, or any mobile data-at-rest code. Do NOT use for architecture/layering design or pure language-style/type rules — those have their own skills. Trigger keywords — SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, SSRF, IDOR, path traversal, insecure deserialization, hardcoded secret, secret in logs, PII leak, sanitize, encode, deny-by-default authz, input validation, TLS, certificate pinning, Keychain, Keystore, clipboard/screenshot leak, key store.
- core:spec-implement: Orchestrate a tiered generator-verifier loop to implement a tightly-specified change cheaply — a strong-tier orchestrator writes the spec and rules, dispatches the cheap-tier executor agent to generate the code, then dispatches the matching strong-tier review agent to verify it, looping until the verifier is clean. Use when you have a SMALL, well-specified, mechanical implementation task (scaffold a component to a schema, boilerplate to a contract, stubs to a spec) and want to route generation to a cheap model while keeping verification strong. Trigger keywords — implement to spec, scaffold, generate to contract, model routing, cheap generate strong verify, generator-verifier, tiered agents. Do NOT use for ambiguous/design work (do it yourself on the strong model), for trivial one-liners (a single strong pass is cheaper than orchestrating), or for pure review with no generation (use pr-review).
- core:testing-behavior: Guidance for writing and reviewing automated tests that catch real bugs — test observable behavior through public APIs, verify resulting state instead of mock call sequences, write tests that survive refactoring, judge suite strength by mutation rather than coverage %, and treat flaky tests as defects. Use when writing unit/integration tests, deciding what to assert, reviewing a test file or PR's tests, debugging a flaky or brittle test, choosing mocks vs fakes, or interpreting a coverage report. Do NOT use for language-specific test-runner setup (pytest/jest/XCTest config) or for non-test code style.
- kotlin:android-architecture: Native-Android app architecture (Google's recommended layered architecture) — load when reading/writing/reviewing native-Android app/feature module code (androidx.*/android.* imports, Activity/Fragment/Service/ViewModel, an :app or :feature module). Covers the UI/domain/data layers and one-way dependency direction Data <- Domain <- UI; single source of truth (the SSOT owns a data type, exposes it immutably, is its only mutator); unidirectional data flow (state down, events up); keeping app logic out of short-lived OS-owned Activities/Fragments/Services; and confining Context/framework classes behind your own abstractions for testability. Triggers — UI/domain/data layer, ViewModel, repository, single source of truth, SSOT, unidirectional data flow, UDF, Activity, Context. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain shared code (use kmp-multiplatform); this is the layering overview, so for depth use android-ui-layer / android-data-layer / android-modularization / jetpack-compose, and for plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:android-data-layer: Native-Android data layer (repositories + data sources) — load when reading/writing/reviewing a native-Android repository, data source, Room/Retrofit/DataStore class, or DI wiring in an app/feature module. Covers the repository as the data layer's only public API (other layers never touch data sources directly); naming (DataType+Repository; DataType+Source+DataSource e.g. NewsRemoteDataSource); one single source of truth per type (offline-first local DB preferred); suspend for one-shot and Flow for streams; immutable exposed models; main-safety via withContext(ioDispatcher) where Dispatchers.IO IS correct (unlike commonMain); errors as Result/custom exceptions; Hilt constructor injection; fakes over mocks. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain shared code (Ktor/SQLDelight/Dispatchers.Default — use kmp-multiplatform/kmp-interop); for the overview use android-architecture, UI state android-ui-layer, modules android-modularization, Compose jetpack-compose, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:android-modularization: Native-Android Gradle modularization (multi-module app structure) — load when reading/writing/reviewing native-Android module boundaries: Gradle build files (build.gradle(.kts) with implementation/api project dependencies), an :app / :feature / :core / :data module, or navigation between features. Covers low coupling and high cohesion; the common module types (app/feature/data/core); the rule that feature modules never depend on other feature modules (the app module mediates, usually via the navigation graph); keeping each module's public surface minimal with Kotlin internal; preferring Gradle implementation over api to avoid leaking transitive deps; and passing primitive IDs (not whole objects) across boundaries. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain source-set layout (a different axis — use kmp-multiplatform/kmp-structure); for in-app layering use android-architecture, UI state android-ui-layer, repositories android-data-layer, Compose jetpack-compose, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:android-ui-layer: Native-Android UI-layer state holders (ViewModel + UI state) — load when reading/writing/reviewing a native-Android ViewModel or screen-level state in an app/feature module (androidx.lifecycle.ViewModel / viewModelScope / StateFlow imports; keywords ViewModel, UiState, collectAsStateWithLifecycle, repeatOnLifecycle, main-safe). Covers the ViewModel as screen-level state holder (survives configuration changes, main-safe, holds NO View/Context/lifecycle reference); modeling UI state as one immutable data class (or a sealed UiState when states are genuinely exclusive); exposing it via read-only StateFlow; and consuming it lifecycle-aware via collectAsStateWithLifecycle (Compose) or repeatOnLifecycle (Views) so collection stops in the background. Do NOT use for KMP commonMain shared code (use kmp-multiplatform); for the overview use android-architecture, repositories android-data-layer, Compose recomposition/side-effects jetpack-compose, Compose-MP UI kmp-compose-mp-ui, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:jetpack-compose: Native-Android Jetpack Compose UI discipline — load when reading/writing/reviewing @Composable code in a native-Android app/feature module (androidx.compose.* imports). Covers state hoisting (stateless composable, value down / events up); recomposition and stability (@Stable/@Immutable, stable params that let Compose skip, unstable collections, stable lambdas); the side-effect APIs (LaunchedEffect and its key restart, rememberCoroutineScope, DisposableEffect/onDispose, rememberUpdatedState, derivedStateOf, snapshotFlow, produceState); remember vs remember(key) vs rememberSaveable; stable keys for lazy-list items; modifier order and the modifier-parameter convention; slot APIs; previews/testing. Do NOT use for Compose Multiplatform / non-Android targets (Skia canvas, UIKitView, iOS/desktop/web — use kmp-compose-mp-ui) or KMP commonMain shared code (kmp-multiplatform); for the architecture overview use android-architecture, ViewModel/UI-state rules android-ui-layer, plain Kotlin style kotlin-style.
- kotlin:kmp-compose-mp-ui: Depth guidance for Compose Multiplatform UI across non-Android targets (iOS, desktop, web/Wasm). Covers the central fact that Compose MP renders via a Skiko/Skia canvas, not native UIKit/SwiftUI widgets, and what follows (identical look by default, native-view interop, simulated-native iOS scroll physics since 1.8.0, on-device verification of canvas/interop/accessibility); choosing Compose MP vs native UI per target; stability (iOS Stable since 1.8.0, desktop Stable, Web/Wasm Beta); resources, fonts, density; navigation. Use when building or reviewing shared Compose UI for iOS/desktop/web, deciding Compose MP vs SwiftUI/native, debugging gestures or scroll feel on iOS, handling images/fonts/strings, or wiring shared navigation. Trigger keywords — Compose Multiplatform, Skiko, desktop Compose, Compose for Web, Wasm, UIKitView, compose-resources, navigation. Do NOT use for Android-only Jetpack Compose, non-UI logic (use kmp-structure), or Swift/Kotlin interop (use kmp-interop).
- kotlin:kmp-interop: Depth guidance for Kotlin <-> Swift/Objective-C interop and per-platform networking in KMP. Covers refining the ObjC header Kotlin exports to Swift (@HiddenFromObjC, @ObjCName, @ShouldRefineInSwift), why not to expose Flow directly to Swift (use SKIE) and that suspend->Swift async is officially experimental, exported-surface quirks (top-level funcs become <FileName>Kt classes, generics only on classes, no default args), and Ktor with ktor-client-core in commonMain plus an engine per platform (Darwin/OkHttp/CIO). Use when designing the API a Swift/iOS app consumes from shared Kotlin, debugging an awkward generated Swift signature, deciding how to bridge Flow or suspend to Swift, or wiring the Ktor client. Trigger keywords — Swift interop, Objective-C, @ObjCName, @ShouldRefineInSwift, SKIE, Flow to Swift, suspend async, Ktor, Darwin, OkHttp. Do NOT use for shared logic structure (use kmp-structure), Compose UI (use kmp-compose-mp-ui), or everyday Kotlin language style (use kotlin-style).
- kotlin:kmp-multiplatform: Kotlin Multiplatform framework rules for shared code — load when reading, writing, or reviewing files under a commonMain or commonTest source set (auto-scoped to **/commonMain/**/*.kt and **/commonTest/**/*.kt), or on demand for KMP layout questions. Covers where shared code lives and the one-way platform->common dependency, what to share vs keep native, the commonMain-only coroutine constraint (Dispatchers.Default not IO, because IO is JVM/Native-only and breaks JS/Wasm), the expect/actual escalation ladder, and commonTest using kotlin.test only (no JUnit, which breaks Native). Keywords — KMP, multiplatform, commonMain, commonTest, expect, actual, source set, Dispatchers in common code, JS, Wasm. Do NOT use for native-Android-only code (there Dispatchers.IO is correct — use the android skills), everyday Kotlin language style (kotlin-style), source-set depth (kmp-structure), Compose-MP UI (kmp-compose-mp-ui), or Swift interop (kmp-interop).

Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.

5	
6	# iOS Testing
7	
8	Testing patterns for Swift and SwiftUI apps.
9	
10	## Unit Tests
11	
12	### Basic Unit Test
13	
14	```swift
15	import XCTest
16	@testable import MyApp
17	
18	class UserViewModelTests: XCTestCase {
19	    var sut: UserViewModel!
20	    var mockService: MockUserService!
21	
22	    override func setUp() {
23	        super.setUp()
24	        mockService = MockUserService()
25	        sut = UserViewModel(service: mockService)
26	    }
27	
28	    override func tearDown() {
29	        sut = nil
30	        mockService = nil
31	        super.tearDown()
32	    }
33	
34	    func testLoadUsers_whenSuccessful_populatesUsers() async throws {
35	        // Given
36	        let expectedUsers = [User.mock1, User.mock2]
37	        mockService.usersToReturn = expectedUsers
38	
39	        // When
40	        await sut.loadUsers()
41	
42	        // Then
43	        XCTAssertEqual(sut.users, expectedUsers)
44	        XCTAssertFalse(sut.isLoading)
45	        XCTAssertNil(sut.errorMessage)
46	    }
47	
48	    func testLoadUsers_whenFailure_setsErrorMessage() async throws {
49	        // Given
50	        mockService.shouldThrowError = true
51	
52	        // When
53	        await sut.loadUsers()
54	
55	        // Then
56	        XCTAssertTrue(sut.users.isEmpty)
57	        XCTAssertNotNil(sut.errorMessage)
58	    }
59	}
60	```
61	
62	### Mocking
63	
64	```swift
65	// ✅ Protocol-based mocking
66	protocol UserServiceProtocol {
67	    func getUsers() async throws -> [User]
68	}
69	
70	class MockUserService: UserServiceProtocol {
71	    var usersToReturn: [User] = []
72	    var shouldThrowError = false
73	    var getUsersCalled = false
74	
75	    func getUsers() async throws -> [User] {
76	        getUsersCalled = true
77	        if shouldThrowError {
78	            throw NetworkError.noConnection
79	        }
80	        return usersToReturn
81	    }
82	}
83	
84	// ✅ Verify method calls
85	func testRefreshButton_callsService() async {
86	    // When
87	    await sut.refresh()
88	
89	    // Then
90	    XCTAssertTrue(mockService.getUsersCalled)
91	}
92	```
93	
94	## Async Testing
95	
96	```swift
97	func testAsyncOperation_completesSuccessfully() async throws {
98	    // Given
99	    let expectation = expectation(description: "Async completes")
100	
101	    // When
102	    Task {
103	        await sut.asyncOperation()
104	        expectation.fulfill()
105	    }
106	
107	    // Then
108	    await fulfillment(of: [expectation], timeout: 1.0)
109	}
110	
111	// ✅ Swift async/await
112	func testAsyncFetch_returnsUsers() async throws {
113	    let users = try await sut.fetchUsers()
114	    XCTAssertFalse(users.isEmpty)
115	}
116	```
117	
118	## Property Testing
119	
120	```swift
121	func testUserValidation_validEmails() {
122	    let validEmails = [
123	        "test@example.com",
124	        "user.name@example.co.uk",
125	        "user+tag@example.com"
126	    ]
127	
128	    for email in validEmails {
129	        XCTAssertTrue(Validator.isValidEmail(email), "Failed for: \(email)")
130	    }
131	}
132	
133	func testUserValidation_invalidEmails() {
134	    let invalidEmails = [
135	        "invalid",
136	        "@example.com",
137	        "user@",
138	        "user @example.com"
139	    ]
140	
141	    for email in invalidEmails {
142	        XCTAssertFalse(Validator.isValidEmail(email), "Passed for: \(email)")
143	    }
144	}
145	```
146	
147	## UI Tests
148	
149	### Basic UI Test
150	
151	```swift
152	import XCTest
153	
154	class LoginUITests: XCTestCase {
155	    var app: XCUIApplication!
156	
157	    override func setUp() {
158	        super.setUp()
159	        continueAfterFailure = false
160	        app = XCUIApplication()
161	        app.launchArguments = ["--uitesting"]
162	        app.launch()
163	    }
164	
165	    func testLoginButton_enabledWhenFieldsFilled() {
166	        // When
167	        let emailField = app.textFields["emailField"]
168	        let passwordField = app.secureTextFields["passwordField"]
169	        let loginButton = app.buttons["loginButton"]
170	
171	        // Then
172	        XCTAssertFalse(loginButton.isEnabled)
173	
174	        // When
175	        emailField.tap()
176	        emailField.typeText("test@example.com")
177	
178	        passwordField.tap()
179	        passwordField.typeText("password123")
180	
181	        // Then
182	        XCTAssertTrue(loginButton.isEnabled)
183	    }
184	
185	    func testSuccessfulLogin_navigatesToHome() {
186	        // Given
187	        app.textFields["emailField"].tap()
188	        app.textFields["emailField"].typeText("test@example.com")
189	
190	        app.secureTextFields["passwordField"].tap()
191	        app.secureTextFields["passwordField"].typeText("password123")
192	
193	        // When
194	        app.buttons["loginButton"].tap()
195	
196	        // Then
197	        XCTAssertTrue(app.staticTexts["welcomeMessage"].exists)
198	    }
199	}
200	```
201	
202	### Snapshot Testing
203	
204	```swift
205	// ✅ Using View snapshot testing
206	import SwiftUI
207	import XCTest
208	
209	struct UserCard_Previews: PreviewProvider {
210	    static var previews: some View {
211	        UserCard(user: .mock)
212	    }
213	}
214	
215	// Snapshot test
216	func testUserCard_snapshot() {
217	    let view = UserCard(user: .mock)
218	    assertSnapshot(matching: view, as: .image(layout: .sizeThatFits))
219	}
220	```
221	
222	## Testing SwiftUI Views
223	
224	```swift
225	import XCTest
226	import ViewInspector  // https://github.com/nalexn/ViewInspector
227	
228	class UserRowTests: XCTestCase {
229	    func testUserRow_displaysUserName() throws {
230	        let user = User(id: "1", name: "John Doe", email: "john@example.com")
231	        let view = UserRow(user: user)
232	
233	        let text = try view.inspect().find(ViewType.Text.self).string()
234	        XCTAssertEqual(text, "John Doe")
235	    }
236	
237	    func testUserRow_tapping_callsAction() throws {
238	        let user = User(id: "1", name: "John", email: "john@example.com")
239	        var tapped = false
240	        let view = UserRow(user: user, onTap: { tapped = true })
241	
242	        try view.inspect().find(ViewType.Button.self).tap()
243	
244	        XCTAssertTrue(tapped)
245	    }
246	}
247	```
248	
249	## Test Helpers
250	
251	```swift
252	// ✅ Test doubles
253	extension User {
254	    static let mock1 = User(id: "1", name: "John", email: "john@example.com")
255	    static let mock2 = User(id: "2", name: "Jane", email: "jane@example.com")
256	}
257	
258	// ✅ Wait helpers
259	func waitForElementToExist(
260	    _ element: XCUIElement,
261	    timeout: TimeInterval = 5.0
262	) -> Bool {
263	    let existsPredicate = NSPredicate(format: "exists == true")
264	    let expectation = expectation(for: existsPredicate, evaluatedWith: element)
265	
266	    let result = XCTWaiter.wait(for: [expectation], timeout: timeout)
267	    return result == .completed
268	}
269	```
270	
271	## Performance Tests
272	
273	```swift
274	func testUserParsing_performance() {
275	    let jsonData = largeUserJSONData
276	
277	    measure {
278	        _ = try? JSONDecoder().decode([User].self, from: jsonData)
279	    }
280	}
281	```
282	
283	## Test Organization
284	
285	```
286	Tests/
287	├── Unit/
288	│   ├── ViewModels/
289	│   │   ├── HomeViewModelTests.swift
290	│   │   └── ProfileViewModelTests.swift
291	│   ├── Services/
292	│   │   ├── UserServiceTests.swift
293	│   │   └── NetworkServiceTests.swift
294	│   └── Models/
295	│       └── UserTests.swift
296	├── UI/
297	│   ├── LoginUITests.swift
298	│   └── HomeUITests.swift
299	└── Mocks/
300	    ├── MockUserService.swift
301	    └── MockNetworkService.swift
302	```
303	
304	---
305	
306	**Remember**: Tests are your safety net. Write them first (TDD) or alongside your code, but always maintain them.

2	name: mobile-verification
3	description: Automated testing workflow with pass@k metrics for mobile development. Detects flaky tests and ensures code reliability.
4	---
5	
6	# Mobile Verification Skill
7	
8	Comprehensive testing workflow with pass@k metrics for Android development reliability.
9	
10	## Philosophy
11	
12	**Single test runs lie.**
13	
14	A test that passes once might fail tomorrow. Verification loops run tests multiple times to reveal:
15	- Flaky tests (timing issues, async problems)
16	- Intermittent failures (resource contention)
17	- Reliability trends (improving vs degrading)
18	
19	## Pass@k Explained
20	
21	Pass@k = proportion of test iterations that passed
22	
23	```
24	Pass@3(test) = tests_passed / 3
25	
26	testLogin(): ✓✓✓ → Pass@3 = 3/3 = 1.0 (100%)
27	testLogout(): ✓✓✗ → Pass@3 = 2/3 = 0.67 (67%)
28	testRefresh(): ✗✗✗ → Pass@3 = 0/3 = 0.0 (0%)
29	```
30	
31	## Verification Levels
32	
33	### Quick Verification (k=2)
34	```
35	Purpose: Fast feedback during development
36	Usage: /mobile-verify --k=2
37	Time: ~2 minutes
38	When: After small changes, before commit
39	```
40	
41	### Standard Verification (k=3)
42	```
43	Purpose: Standard confidence level
44	Usage: /mobile-verify --k=3
45	Time: ~5 minutes
46	When: Before push, after feature complete
47	```
48	
49	### Thorough Verification (k=5)
50	```
51	Purpose: High confidence, flaky detection
52	Usage: /mobile-verify --k=5
53	Time: ~10 minutes
54	When: Before release, after refactor
55	```
56	
57	### Release Verification (k=10)
58	```
59	Purpose: Maximum confidence
60	Usage: /mobile-verify --k=10
61	Time: ~20 minutes
62	When: Production release, critical bugs
63	```
64	
65	## Test Type Strategies
66	
67	### Unit Tests (JUnit)
68	
69	**Characteristics:**
70	- Fast: ~1-2 seconds per test
71	- Isolated: No Android dependencies
72	- Reliable: Should be Pass@k = 1.0
73	
74	**Target Pass@k:** ≥ 0.95 (95%)
75	
76	**Common Flaky Causes:**
77	- Async operations without proper waiting
78	- Date/time dependencies
79	- Random data generation
80	- Static state leakage
81	
82	**Fix Strategies:**
83	```kotlin
84	// Bad: Flaky
85	@Test
86	fun testLoadData() {
87	    viewModel.loadData()
88	    assert(viewModel.state.value is Loaded)
89	}
90	
91	// Good: Stable
92	@Test
93	fun testLoadData() = runTest {
94	    viewModel.loadData()
95	    advanceUntilIdle()
96	    assert(viewModel.state.value is Loaded)
97	}
98	```
99	
100	### UI Tests (Espresso)
101	
102	**Characteristics:**
103	- Slow: ~5-10 seconds per test
104	- Device-dependent: Need emulator/device
105	- Fragile: UI changes break tests
106	
107	**Target Pass@k:** ≥ 0.80 (80%)
108	
109	**Common Flaky Causes:**
110	- Idling resource not registered
111	- Animation interference
112	- Screen rotation
113	- Network timeouts
114	
115	**Fix Strategies:**
116	```kotlin
117	// Register idling resources
118	@IdlingResource
119	val countingIdlingResource = CountingIdlingResource("api")
120	
121	// Disable animations
122	@get:Rule
123	val disableAnimationsRule = DisableAnimationsRule()
124	```
125	
126	### Compose Tests
127	
128	**Characteristics:**
129	- Fast: ~1-3 seconds per test
130	- UI-level: Tests Composable behavior
131	- Modern: Uses Compose Testing framework
132	
133	**Target Pass@k:** ≥ 0.90 (90%)
134	
135	**Common Flaky Causes:**
136	- Recomposition timing
137	- State hoisting issues
138	- Animation interference
139	
140	**Fix Strategies:**
141	```kotlin
142	@Composable
143	fun TestComposable(content: @Composable () -> Unit) {
144	    CompositionLocalProvider(
145	        LocalInspectionMode provides true
146	    ) {
147	        content()
148	    }
149	}
150	```
151	
152	## Verification Workflow
153	
154	### During Development
155	
156	```bash
157	# 1. Write test
158	# 2. Quick verify
159	/mobile-verify --class=NewTest --k=2
160	
161	# 3. Fix if fails
162	# 4. Standard verify
163	/mobile-verify --class=NewTest --k=3
164	```
165	
166	### Before Commit
167	
168	```bash
169	# Verify changed modules only
170	/mobile-verify --module=$(git diff --name-only | head -1) --k=2
171	```
172	
173	### Before Push
174	
175	```bash
176	# Full verification
177	/mobile-verify --k=3
178	```
179	
180	### Before Release
181	
182	```bash
183	# Thorough verification with flaky detection
184	/mobile-verify --k=5 --flaky
185	```
186	
187	## Interpreting Results
188	
189	### Pass@k Scores
190	
191	| Score | Meaning | Action |
192	|-------|---------|--------|
193	| 1.0 | Perfect | Celebrate |
194	| 0.8-0.9 | Excellent | Monitor |
195	| 0.6-0.7 | Good | Investigate |
196	| 0.4-0.5 | Fair | Fix needed |
197	| 0.0-0.3 | Poor | Block release |
198	
199	### Trends
200	
201	Track pass@k over time:
202	
203	```
204	Week 1: Pass@3 = 0.85
205	Week 2: Pass@3 = 0.87  ↗ Improving
206	Week 3: Pass@3 = 0.82  ↘ Degraded - investigate!
207	Week 4: Pass@3 = 0.88  ↗ Recovered
208	```
209	
210	### Flaky Test Patterns
211	
212	| Pattern | Likely Cause |
213	|---------|--------------|
214	| Fails on iteration 1 only | Cold start issue |
215	| Fails randomly | Async timing |
216	| Fails on specific iteration | Resource leak |
217	| Fails in parallel only | Shared state |
218	
219	## Fixing Flaky Tests
220	
221	### Step 1: Identify Pattern
222	
223	```bash
224	/mobile-verify --flaky --k=10
225	```
226	
227	Look for patterns in failures.
228	
229	### Step 2: Add Diagnostics
230	
231	```kotlin
232	@Test
233	fun flakyTest() = runTest {
234	    val startTime = System.currentTimeMillis()
235	    // ... test code ...
236	    val duration = System.currentTimeMillis() - startTime
237	    Log.d("Test", "Duration: $duration ms")  // Check for timing issues
238	}
239	```
240	
241	### Step 3: Apply Fix
242	
243	Common fixes:
244	- Add `advanceUntilIdle()` for coroutines
245	- Add `IdlingResource` for network
246	- Disable animations for UI tests
247	- Use `@UiThreadTest` for main thread work
248	- Add explicit waits for async operations
249	
250	### Step 4: Verify Fix
251	
252	```bash
253	/mobile-verify --class=FixedTest --k=5
254	```
255	
256	Target: Pass@5 = 1.0
257	
258	## Integration
259	
260	### With Checkpoints
261	
262	Create checkpoint before verification:
263	```bash
264	/mobile-checkpoint save pre-verify
265	/mobile-verify --k=3
266	```
267	
268	### With Memory
269	
270	Track pass@k in memory:
271	```json
272	{
273	    "test-coverage": {
274	        "passAt3": 0.87,
275	        "trend": "improving",
276	        "flakyTests": []
277	    }
278	}
279	```
280	
281	### With Instincts
282	
283	Learn testing patterns:
284	```json
285	{
286	    "id": "test-coroutine-async",
287	    "description": "Always use runTest + advanceUntilIdle for ViewModel tests",
288	    "confidence": 0.95
289	}
290	```
291	
292	## Thresholds by Context
293	
294	| Context | Pass@k Threshold | Rationale |
295	|---------|------------------|-----------|
296	| Unit tests | 0.95 | Should be deterministic |
297	| UI tests | 0.80 | More fragile, device-dependent |
298	| Compose tests | 0.90 | Better than Espresso, more stable |
299	| Integration tests | 0.70 | Complex, more variables |
300	| E2E tests | 0.60 | Full system, many variables |
301	
302	## Best Practices
303	
304	1. **Start High, Go Low**: Use k=5 for investigation, k=3 for routine
305	2. **Fix Flaky Fast**: Don't tolerate flaky tests
306	3. **Track Trends**: Monitor pass@k over time
307	4. **Context Matters**: UI tests can have lower thresholds than unit
308	5. **Block Release**: Failed verification should block releases
309	
310	---
311	
312	**Remember**: A test that sometimes passes is worse than no test at all. It gives false confidence.
313

1	---
2	name: compose-ui-testing-patterns
3	description: Use when writing or reviewing Jetpack Compose UI tests, screenshot tests, previews, semantics assertions, fake image loading, keyboard input, focus assertions, interaction state (hover/pressed/focused), or tests for plain state-driven UI composables.
4	---
5	
6	# Compose: UI testing patterns
7	
8	## Core principle
9	
10	Test the smallest UI contract that proves the behavior. Prefer plain state-driven UI tests with callbacks. Add integration only when lifecycle, navigation, DI, or platform behavior is the thing under test.
11	
12	## Test target choice
13	
14	| What you need to prove | Test shape |
15	|---|---|
16	| Text, button, loading/error branch, conditional content | Plain UI Compose test |
17	| Callback wiring from click/input | Plain UI Compose test |
18	| Focus navigation or keyboard behavior | Compose test with key input |
19	| Visual layout, clipping, elevation, typography, image composition | Screenshot test |
20	| State holder updates UI correctly | State holder/unit test plus one wiring smoke test |
21	| Hover, pressed, focused, dragged interaction state | Plain UI test with MutableInteractionSource |
22	| Navigation, lifecycle, DI integration | Integration test |
23	
24	## Prefer plain UI tests
25	
26	If the screen has a state holder/UI split, test the plain UI composable:
27	
28	```kotlin
29	composeTestRule.setContent {
30	    ProfileScreen(
31	        state = ProfileUiState(name = "Ada", canSave = true),
32	        onNameChange = {},
33	        onSaveClick = { saved = true },
34	        onBackClick = {},
35	    )
36	}
37	
38	composeTestRule.onNodeWithText("Ada").assertIsDisplayed()
39	composeTestRule.onNodeWithText("Save").performClick()
40	
41	assertThat(saved).isTrue()
42	```
43	
44	This avoids constructing ViewModels, components, repositories, navigation, and dependency graphs for layout behavior.
45	
46	## Semantics first
47	
48	Assert semantics when behavior is semantic:
49	
50	- Text exists: `onNodeWithText`.
51	- Button is enabled/disabled: `assertIsEnabled`, `assertIsNotEnabled`.
52	- Content is selected/focused/toggled: use semantics assertions.
53	- Content is absent: `assertDoesNotExist`.
54	
55	Use test tags for nodes that have no stable user-visible text or where multiple nodes share text. Do not use tags as the first choice for all assertions; user-visible semantics are usually stronger.
56	
57	## Callback testing
58	
59	Use simple counters or captured values:
60	
61	```kotlin
62	var selectedId: String? = null
63	
64	composeTestRule.setContent {
65	    ItemList(
66	        items = listOf(ItemUi("movie-1", "Movie")),
67	        onItemClick = { selectedId = it },
68	    )
69	}
70	
71	composeTestRule.onNodeWithText("Movie").performClick()
72	
73	assertThat(selectedId).isEqualTo("movie-1")
74	```
75	
76	For plain captured callback values, a direct assertion after the action is usually enough. Use `runOnIdle` when the assertion needs Compose to finish applying snapshot state, recomposition, or queued UI work before reading the result.
77	
78	## Interaction state with MutableInteractionSource
79	
80	When a composable's appearance or behavior depends on interaction state (hover, focus, press, drag), inject a `MutableInteractionSource` and emit the desired state directly. Do not try to simulate pointer/mouse events to trigger interaction states — that approach is fragile, environment-dependent, and produces flaky tests.
81	
82	```kotlin
83	val interactionSource = MutableInteractionSource()
84	
85	composeTestRule.setContent {
86	    OutlinedButton(
87	        onClick = {},
88	        interactionSource = interactionSource,
89	    )
90	}
91	
92	// Assert default (un-hovered) state
93	composeTestRule.onNodeWithText("OutlinedButton").assertIsDisplayed()
94	
95	// Emit hover — interactionSource.emit is a suspend function,
96	// so call it from a test coroutine scope.
97	TestScope().launch {
98	    interactionSource.emit(HoverInteraction.Enter())
99	}
100	
101	composeTestRule.waitForIdle()
102	
103	// Assert the visual/semantic change that hover produces
104	// (e.g., border color, elevation, or capture for screenshot test)
105	composeTestRule.onNodeWithText("OutlinedButton").assertIsDisplayed()
106	```
107	
108	The same pattern works for `PressInteraction.Press` / `Release` / `Cancel`, `FocusInteraction.Focus` / `Unfocus`, and `DragInteraction.Start` / `Stop` / `Cancel`. Emit the entry interaction, `waitForIdle`, then assert the result.
109	
110	Key points:
111	
112	- **Always inject `MutableInteractionSource`** rather than relying on the default internal source. This gives you full control over state transitions.
113	- **Emit interactions from a coroutine scope** (e.g. `TestScope().launch { }`) since `emit` is a suspend function. Do not use `LaunchedEffect` — that is a production Compose effect, not a test tool.
114	- **Assert the *result* of the interaction** (visual change, semantic change, enabled state), not the interaction itself. The interaction source is a test *driver*, not the assertion target.
115	- **Use this for screenshot tests too** — emit the interaction state, then capture the screenshot for a deterministic hover/press/focus visual.
116	
117	## Keyboard and focus
118	
119	For keyboard, TV, and desktop UI, drive navigation with the same input model users use (keys/D-pad), not clicks alone. Assert focused semantics, not colors or scale; reserve screenshots for visual focus treatment.
120	
121	Details—focus graph, `FocusRequester`, restoration, key handlers, and test patterns: [`compose-focus-navigation`](../compose-focus-navigation/SKILL.md).
122	
123	## Screenshot tests
124	
125	Use screenshots for visual contracts that semantics cannot prove:
126	
127	- Layout spacing/alignment.
128	- Themed colors, typography, elevation, shadows.
129	- Image composition, gradients, overlays.
130	- Focus highlight appearance.
131	- Loading skeletons or dense visual states.
132	
133	Keep screenshot state deterministic:
134	
135	- Use fixed state data.
136	- Freeze clocks or animation progress when possible.
137	- Replace network/image loading with fake or preview handlers.
138	- Avoid asserting dynamic text such as current time unless controlled.
139	
140	## Fake images and platform services
141	
142	When image content is irrelevant, fake the loader and assert the requested model if that is the behavior. The exact hook depends on your image library; a project helper might look like this:
143	
144	```kotlin
145	val requestedModels = mutableListOf<Any?>()
146	
147	// Example helper, not a Compose API.
148	setContentWithFakeImageLoader { request ->
149	    requestedModels += request.data
150	    errorPainter()
151	}
152	```
153	
154	When image appearance matters, provide a deterministic local painter/bitmap instead of network data.
155	
156	## Common mistakes
157	
158	| Mistake | Fix |
159	|---|---|
160	| Constructing full app graph to test an error row | Test plain UI with `state = Error` |
161	| Testing click behavior through a ViewModel mock | Pass a callback and assert it was invoked |
162	| Screenshot test for simple text presence | Use semantics assertion |
163	| Semantics test for padding/color/focus ring | Use screenshot test |
164	| Test tags everywhere | Prefer text/content description/role when stable |
165	| UI test depends on real image loading/network/time | Fake or freeze the source |
166	| Simulating hover/press/focus with mouse or touch events | Inject `MutableInteractionSource` and emit the interaction |
167	| Relying on the default `InteractionSource` in tests | Pass `MutableInteractionSource` so you can control state |
168	| TV/keyboard UI tested with `performClick` only | Use key input and focus assertions; see [compose-focus-navigation](../compose-focus-navigation/SKILL.md) |
169	
170	## Red flags during review
171	
172	- "This UI test is flaky because images load slowly."
173	- A test uses production DI for simple rendering.
174	- A screenshot has random dates, clocks, remote images, or live data.
175	- Assertions only check that a node exists after performing an action, not that the callback/state change happened.
176	- Focus behavior is visually inspected but not asserted.
177	- A test uses `performMouseInput` or touch injection to trigger hover/press states instead of `MutableInteractionSource.emit`.
178	- A composable accepts `interactionSource` but tests don't inject `MutableInteractionSource`.

9	---
10	
11	# Android Testing
12	
13	Android-specific testing on a **test-first** foundation. This reference focuses on the test-first discipline plus the Compose-test traps that are easy to get wrong, not the basics of the three tiers, fakes over mocks, `runTest`, or Given-When-Then naming.
14	
15	## Test-first (the foundation)
16	
17	- **No production code without a failing test first.** Write the test, watch it fail (RED), write the minimal code to pass (GREEN), then refactor. A behaviour you never watched fail isn't proven.
18	- **A bug isn't fixed until a test that was red *because of the bug* is green.**
19	
20	This layers on top of any dedicated TDD discipline skill (`superpowers:test-driven-development`, `ace:test-driven-development`) but requires none. For *bootstrapping* the test stack from scratch (test DI, JUnit/Robolectric/Roborazzi/Paparazzi selection, the instrumented runner, Compose Preview Screenshot Testing, UI Automator, Jacoco), see Google's official [`testing-setup`](https://github.com/android/skills/tree/main/testing/testing-setup) skill (`android skills add testing-setup`).
21	
22	## Compose tests now default to `StandardTestDispatcher`
23	
24	`createComposeRule()` / `runComposeUiTest {}` default to `StandardTestDispatcher` (matching `kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest`) — **there is no separate "v2" package.** It's gated by `androidx.compose.ui.test.ComposeUiTestFlags.isStandardTestDispatcherSupportEnabled` (defaults to `true`), so the regular `androidx.compose.ui.test.junit4.createComposeRule` already uses it. To pin a scheduler, pass it through: `createComposeRule(effectContext = StandardTestDispatcher())`. Under this default, a `LaunchedEffect` that previously ran eagerly (the old `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` behaviour) may need an explicit `mainClock.advanceTimeBy(0)` / `runCurrent()` to drain queued work; set the flag `false` only to temporarily restore the legacy behaviour.
25	
26	**Two-schedulers trap** (the one coroutine-test gotcha worth stating): a `MainDispatcherRule`'s `TestDispatcher` and the dispatcher `runTest { }` creates have **separate** `TestCoroutineScheduler`s. Pass `mainRule.dispatcher` into `runTest(mainRule.dispatcher)` so `Dispatchers.Main` and the test body share one — otherwise `advanceUntilIdle()` flushes only one and assertions race the ViewModel.
27	
28	## Semantics first, `testTag` as fallback
29	
30	Prefer user-visible semantics over `testTag` — real users and screen readers see semantics; `testTag` is invisible to everyone except tests. Selector priority: (1) `onNodeWithText`; (2) `onNodeWithContentDescription`; (3) role/state matchers (`hasClickAction()`, `isSelected()`, `isFocused()`, `isEnabled()`); (4) `onNodeWithTag` **only** when there's no stable user-visible text or it's duplicated/ambiguous (lists of identical rows, per-locale copy, multiple instances). A text assertion survives refactors and exercises accessibility; a `testTag` assertion breaks the moment the tag changes and misses the user-facing regression.
31	
32	*(Counterview worth knowing: [skydoves/android-testing-skills](https://github.com/skydoves/android-testing-skills) argues tag-first for i18n robustness, backed by androidx/material3's own 1825 : 424 : 46 `testTag` : `onNodeWithText` : `onNodeWithContentDescription` ratio. Defensible if you have separate accessibility coverage; this skill defaults to semantics-first because it catches a class of bugs `testTag` never can.)*
33	
34	## Callbacks as test surfaces
35	
36	A composable's contract is "render state, emit callbacks" — test exactly that; don't route the assertion through a ViewModel mock.
37	
38	```kotlin
39	@Test fun `tapping article row invokes onArticleClick with id`() {
40	    var clickedId: String? = null
41	    composeTestRule.setContent { ArticleRow(Article(id = "42", title = "Hello"), onArticleClick = { clickedId = it }) }
42	    composeTestRule.onNodeWithText("Hello").performClick()
43	    assertEquals("42", clickedId)
44	}
45	```
46	
47	## Choosing the test shape — the smallest contract that proves the behaviour
48	
49	| Proving | Shape |
50	|---|---|
51	| Text rendered, conditional content, loading/error branches, callback wiring | Plain UI Compose test (state + callbacks, no graph) |
52	| Focus navigation, keyboard, TV/D-pad | Compose test with `performKeyInput` + `assertIsFocused()` (see `compose/references/focus-navigation.md`) |
53	| Visual contract semantics can't prove — spacing, themed colour, typography, elevation, gradients, skeletons | Screenshot test, one per meaningful state |
54	| State holder updates UI correctly | State-holder unit test + ONE wiring smoke test |
55	| Lifecycle, navigation, or DI integration itself | Integration test (`createAndroidComposeRule`, Hilt rule, real graph) |
56	
57	**Test clock vs wall clock:** for any Compose-state-observable condition use `mainClock.advanceTimeUntil(ms) { state.value == Done }` (deterministic, fast); use `rule.waitUntil(ms) { … }` only for non-Compose conditions (`Job.isCompleted`, an external counter). Mixing the two in one test is a common flake source.
58	
59	**Animation tests need `mainClock.autoAdvance = false` set *before* `setContent`** — otherwise the framework's `InfiniteAnimationPolicy` throws `CancellationException` on indeterminate animations, and finite animations finish in one auto-advanced burst with no observable intermediate state. After pausing, drive frames with `advanceTimeByFrame()` (kick-off) then `advanceTimeBy(durationMillis)`.
60	
61	**Screenshot determinism:** fixed state data (no current time, random seeds, or remote URLs in the screenshot path); frozen clocks (`Clock.fixed(...)`) and animation progress; a fake image loader for image-heavy screens (Coil 3's test double: `LocalImageLoader provides FakeImageLoader(LocalContext.current)`, or `setContentWithFakeImageLoader { … }`); one shot per meaningful state (loading / error / success / empty), not one per UI element.

1	---
2	name: android-debugging
3	description: >
4	  Use when debugging Android or KMP issues — Android-specific techniques covering Logcat, ADB,
5	  ANR traces, R8 stack trace decoding, memory leaks, Gradle build failures, and Compose
6	  recomposition bugs, on a root-cause-first foundation.
7	---
8	
9	# Android Debugging
10	
11	## Overview
12	
13	Android-specific evidence-gathering and investigation techniques on a root-cause-first foundation.
14	
15	**Root-cause-first foundation:**
16	- **No fix before the root cause is found.** Investigate first — reproduce, gather evidence (observed values, not assumed), trace the cause. Patching a symptom you don't understand creates two bugs.
17	- **Three failed guesses ⇒ stop and question the architecture** rather than guessing again.
18	
19	The Android-specific tools below serve that investigation. *Optional:* if you run a dedicated debugging-discipline skill (e.g. `superpowers:systematic-debugging` or `ace:systematic-debugging`), this layers on top of it — but it requires none.
20	
21	## Evidence-Gathering by Problem Type
22	
23	### Crashes & Exceptions
24	
25	```bash
26	# Stream crash logs filtered by app package
27	adb logcat --pid=$(adb shell pidof -s com.example.app)
28	
29	# Save full logcat to file for analysis
30	adb logcat -d > crash_log.txt
31	
32	# Filter by tag
33	adb logcat -s "YourTag:E"
34	```
35	
36	Key logcat log levels: `V` (verbose) `D` (debug) `I` (info) `W` (warn) `E` (error) `F` (fatal)
37	
38	Read the **full stack trace** — the root cause is usually at the bottom of the `Caused by:` chain, not the top-level exception.
39	
40	### ANR (Application Not Responding)
41	
42	ANRs mean the main thread was blocked. Evidence:
43	
44	```bash
45	# Pull ANR trace from device
46	adb pull /data/anr/traces.txt ./anr_traces.txt
47	
48	# Or stream while reproducing
49	adb logcat -s "ActivityManager:E" | grep -A 30 "ANR in"
50	```
51	
52	Look for: `main` thread in state `MONITOR` (waiting for a lock) or blocking I/O on `main`. Trace backward to find what holds the lock.
53	
54	**Common causes:** Database/network call on main thread, `runBlocking` on main thread, deadlock between coroutine scopes.
55	
56	### Memory Leaks
57	
58	Add [LeakCanary](https://square.github.io/leakcanary/) to `debugImplementation`. It surfaces leak traces automatically in a notification.
59	
60	Read the leak trace top-to-bottom: the first bold line is the leaking object, the path shows what's holding the reference. Fix by clearing the reference in the appropriate lifecycle callback.
61	
62	```bash
63	# Dump heap manually for Android Profiler analysis
64	adb shell am dumpheap com.example.app /data/local/tmp/heap.hprof
65	adb pull /data/local/tmp/heap.hprof ./heap.hprof
66	```
67	
68	### Performance Trace Investigation (Perfetto)
69	
70	For bottleneck investigation across CPU, graphics, I/O, IPC, memory, or power — beyond what Logcat and ANR traces show — capture a Perfetto trace and query it with SQL.
71	
72	**Measure before you fix.** For performance regressions, logs usually mislead — capture a *baseline* measurement before changing anything, then bisect against it. A trace tells you where time goes; only a comparison against a known-good baseline tells you what actually regressed.
73	
74	```bash
75	# Capture a trace (system-level, all categories)
76	adb shell perfetto -c - --txt -o /data/misc/perfetto-traces/trace.pftrace \
77	  <<'EOF'
78	buffers { size_kb: 65536 }
79	data_sources { config { name: "linux.ftrace" } }
80	data_sources { config { name: "android.surfaceflinger.frame" } }
81	duration_ms: 10000
82	EOF
83	
84	adb pull /data/misc/perfetto-traces/trace.pftrace ./
85	```
86	
87	Then open the trace at https://ui.perfetto.dev and run SQL against it (`SELECT name, dur FROM slice WHERE dur > 16e6` for frames slower than 16ms, etc.).
88	
89	For an agent-driven workflow — translating an investigation intent (jank, slow startup, battery drain) into the right Perfetto SQL and iterating across the trace — see Google's [`perfetto-sql`](https://github.com/android/skills/tree/main/profilers/perfetto-sql) and [`perfetto-trace-analysis`](https://github.com/android/skills/tree/main/profilers/perfetto-trace-analysis) skills (`android skills list` to check for a local install; `android skills add perfetto-sql perfetto-trace-analysis` otherwise). They provide Domain Hints (CPU/Graphics/I/O/IPC/Memory/Power), a mandatory scratchpad chain-of-evidence pattern, and `GLOB`-over-`LIKE` query rules.
90	
91	### R8 / ProGuard — Obfuscated Stack Traces
92	
93	Release crash stack traces are obfuscated. Decode them with the mapping file generated at build time.
94	
95	```bash
96	# retrace a crash (AGP 7+)
97	./gradlew :app:retrace --stacktrace-file crash.txt
98	
99	# Or use the retrace CLI directly
100	java -jar retrace.jar mapping.txt crash.txt
101	```
102	
103	Mapping files are in `app/build/outputs/mapping/<variant>/mapping.txt`. Always archive them alongside release builds.
104	
105	If a class is unexpectedly removed or renamed, add a `-keep` rule in `proguard-rules.pro` and verify with:
106	
107	```bash
108	./gradlew :app:assembleRelease
109	# Then inspect: app/build/outputs/mapping/release/usage.txt (removed) and seeds.txt (kept)
110	```
111	
112	For the **inverse problem** — reading obfuscated third-party code or decoding a stack trace from a library where the mapping file isn't yours — `retrace` doesn't apply. Use `jadx --deobf` (consistent renames across the decompiled output) or `jadx --deobf-map` (when the SDK ships a mapping). The [`android-reverse-engineering` plugin](https://github.com/SimoneAvogadro/android-reverse-engineering-skill) covers the full workflow including the anchor-via-strings strategy for navigating obfuscated code by string literals and framework class names that survive obfuscation (check if it's already installed locally first — it ships as `android-reverse-engineering:*` skills).
113	
114	### Gradle Build Failures
115	
116	Read the error from the **bottom up** — Gradle wraps errors in multiple layers.
117	
118	Common patterns:
119	
120	| Error | Investigation |
121	|-------|--------------|
122	| `Manifest merger failed` | Check `app/build/intermediates/merged_manifests/` for the merged output; look for conflicting `android:` attributes |
123	| `Duplicate class` | Run `./gradlew dependencies` and look for the same class in multiple transitive deps; use `exclude` or force a version |
124	| `Could not resolve` | Check repository declarations, VPN/proxy, dependency version exists |
125	| `D8/R8: Type not present` | Missing `keep` rule or desugaring issue; check `minSdk` vs API used |
126	| `KSP / KAPT error` | Look for the processor's own error above the Gradle wrapper message |
127	
128	```bash
129	# Full dependency tree for a configuration
130	./gradlew :app:dependencies --configuration releaseRuntimeClasspath
131	
132	# Run with stacktrace for deeper Gradle errors
133	./gradlew assembleDebug --stacktrace --info 2>&1 | grep -A 20 "FAILED"
134	```
135	
136	### Runtime UI Inspection
137	
138	When a bug is visual (wrong element state, missing content, overlap), dump the layout tree directly instead of reasoning from a screenshot:
139	
140	```bash
141	# Full layout tree as JSON — search by class/text/bounds instead of parsing an image
142	android layout --pretty
143	
144	# Only elements that changed since last call — useful for animations or transient state
145	android layout --diff --pretty
146	
147	# Target a specific device, write to file
148	android layout --device=emulator-5554 -o layout.json
149	```
150	
151	Prefer `android layout` over `adb screencap` whenever the question is "what is the UI state?" rather than "what does it look like?". The JSON tree is grep-able and survives `--diff` state across invocations.
152	
153	### Compose Recomposition Bugs
154	
155	For deeper Compose performance analysis (stability, recomposition skipping, baseline profiles), see `android-skills:compose` → `compose/references/performance.md`.
156	
157	Wrong state or unexpected re-renders:
158	
159	1. **Layout Inspector** (Android Studio) → enable "Show recomposition counts" to identify hot paths. For headless/CLI workflows, `android layout --diff` gives a JSON tree of what changed between frames.
160	2. Add `SideEffect { Log.d("Recompose", "MyComposable recomposed") }` temporarily to confirm
161	3. Check that `State` objects are not created inside the composition (use `remember`)
162	4. Verify `equals()` on state data classes — a new object with same values still triggers recomposition if `equals` is not implemented
163	
164	**Note:** Since Compose compiler 2.0+ (Kotlin 2.0+), strong skipping mode is enabled by default and the compiler automatically memoizes lambdas that capture stable references. Manual `remember {{ }}` wrapping is no longer necessary in most cases. If you see excessive recomposition from lambdas, check whether the captured references are unstable (mutable collections, non-data classes) rather than wrapping in `remember`.
165	
166	(Standard `adb` commands — `devices`, `install -r`, `am start`, `pm clear`, `ps`, `run-as … ls /data/data/<pkg>/` — aren't covered here; for visual-state bugs prefer `android layout` over `screencap` as noted above.)
167	
168	## Multi-Component Evidence Template
169	
170	For issues spanning multiple layers (e.g. Repository → ViewModel → UI):
171	
172	```kotlin
173	// Temporarily instrument each boundary with a UNIQUE run-specific tag
174	// (pick a fresh suffix per session, e.g. DEBUG-a4f2) so the SAME tag both
175	// filters logcat at runtime and greps cleanly at teardown.
176	class UserRepository(...) {
177	    suspend fun fetchUser(id: String): User {
178	        Log.d("DEBUG-a4f2", "Repository: fetching user $id")
179	        val result = api.getUser(id)
180	        Log.d("DEBUG-a4f2", "Repository: received ${result}")
181	        return result
182	    }
183	}
184	```
185	
186	Run once to identify **which layer** produces the bad value. Filter the run at runtime with `adb logcat -s "DEBUG-a4f2"`, then tear the instrumentation back out with a single `grep -rl "DEBUG-a4f2"`. A unique per-session tag is what makes both one-liners work — a shared tag like `DEBUG_LAYER` collides across sessions and leaves orphaned logs behind. Then investigate the implicated layer in isolation before proposing a fix.
187	
188	## Red Flags
189	
190	- Fixing a crash without reading the full `Caused by:` chain
191	- Guessing at an R8 issue without checking the mapping file
192	- Adding `Thread.sleep()` to "fix" an ANR or race condition
193	- Resolving a dependency conflict by adding `exclude` without understanding why the duplicate exists
194	- Fixing a Compose bug by wrapping in `key()` without understanding what triggers recomposition
195	- Leaving temporary instrumentation in the tree — tag every debug log with a unique per-session prefix (e.g. `DEBUG-a4f2`) so cleanup is one `grep`, and remove them all before declaring the fix done

The `awaitItem()` assertions there are already covered by bug 3, so nothing new there. But looking at the `UserRepositoryTest` in the same file, I notice the `repository` field is declared as `private lateinit var` but never actually initialized — there's no `@BeforeEach` setup method, and the test just tries to use it directly.

What's worse, the `@MockK` annotation on `api` also requires `MockKAnnotations.init(this)` to be called, which isn't happening here either. contradictionVerdicts.topic: Test doubles for substituting collaborators: mocks vs fakes
contradictionVerdicts.reasoning: The quoted lines are accurate. ahmed/mobile-testing demonstrates Mockk-based isolation as the default throughout: line 30 `@MockK private lateinit var repository: HomeRepository` with line 41 `coEvery { repository.getItems() } returns ...`, and line 57 `@MockK private lateinit var api: UserApi` with line 61 `coEvery { api.getUser("1") } returns UserDto("1", "John")`. The word 'fake' never appears anywhere in ahmed's testing skills. rcosteira/android-testing line 13 states its foundation as building on '...the three tiers, fakes over mocks, runTest...' — an explicit preference for fakes over mocks. These are genuinely opposing recommendations on the same question (how to substitute collaborators): ahmed's demonstrated default is mocks; rcosteira's stated principle is fakes. This is a real opposing-advice conflict, not a wording/depth difference. The chris supporting citation is also accurate but secondary/tangential: compose-ui-testing-patterns line 161 lists 'Testing click behavior through a ViewModel mock' -> 'Pass a callback and assert it was invoked' — that is really about callback-vs-mock UI test design rather than fakes-vs-mocks collaborator substitution, so it only loosely reinforces the anti-mock direction. The core ahmed-vs-rcosteira conflict is solid.

contradictionVerdicts.topic: Strictness of test-first (must a failing test always precede production code?)
contradictionVerdicts.reasoning: Quotes verified. rcosteira/android-testing line 17: 'No production code without a failing test first. Write the test, watch it fail (RED), write the minimal code to pass (GREEN)... A behaviour you never watched fail isn't proven.' and line 18: 'A bug isn't fixed until a test that was red because of the bug is green.' — strict, no exceptions. ahmed/ios-testing line 306: 'Write them first (TDD) or alongside your code, but always maintain them.' — the 'or alongside your code' explicitly permits writing production code without a preceding failing test. These directly oppose each other on whether test-first is mandatory. Nuance worth recording: ahmed's own Android skill (mobile-testing line 97, 'Write tests first') actually aligns with rcosteira, so the contradiction is specifically between rcosteira and ahmed's iOS skill; ahmed is also internally inconsistent across its two skills. But the finding cites the iOS line precisely and the opposition is real, so CONFIRMED rather than PARTIAL.

bugVerdicts.description: chris compose-ui-testing-patterns: interaction-state example launches interactionSource.emit(...) on a fresh detached TestScope() that is never advanced, so the emit never runs and the hover state is never applied before the assertion.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Code at lines 97-105 verified verbatim: `TestScope().launch { interactionSource.emit(HoverInteraction.Enter()) }` then `composeTestRule.waitForIdle()`. TestScope() is backed by a StandardTestDispatcher/TestCoroutineScheduler which does NOT run queued coroutines eagerly (unlike UnconfinedTestDispatcher) — tasks only run when the scheduler is pumped via runCurrent()/advanceUntilIdle()/advanceTimeBy(). There is no runTest wrapping it and no manual advancement, so the launched coroutine body never executes and emit() never happens. composeTestRule.waitForIdle() synchronizes only Compose's own recomposition/idling, not an unrelated external scheduler. Therefore the comment 'Assert the visual/semantic change that hover produces' would be evaluated against the un-hovered state. This is the skill's flagship/unique technique, so teaching a non-working driver is material. (Ironically the skill correctly warns against LaunchedEffect at line 113 but substitutes an equally non-functional driver.) Severity major is fair.

bugVerdicts.description: ahmed mobile-testing: ViewModel test constructs HomeViewModel(repository) and uses runTest but installs no MainDispatcherRule/Dispatchers.setMain, so a viewModelScope-based ViewModel throws IllegalStateException (Main dispatcher not initialized).
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Lines 29-49 verified; I also confirmed the entire 98-line file contains no MainDispatcherRule, no Dispatchers.setMain, and no JUnit5 equivalent. runTest sets up a TestDispatcher but does NOT replace Dispatchers.Main. A standard MVI ViewModel exposing a StateFlow `state` and processing `onIntent(LoadItems)` launches in viewModelScope, which is bound to Dispatchers.Main.immediate. On the JVM without an Android main looper, Dispatchers.Main is a missing dispatcher that throws IllegalStateException ('Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize...') on dispatch. So `viewModel.onIntent(LoadItems)` (or even construction if init launches) throws. This is exactly the well-known trap rcosteira/android-testing line 26 documents (share mainRule.dispatcher into runTest). CONFIRMED; the only residual dependency is that HomeViewModel uses viewModelScope, which the state/onIntent shape makes overwhelmingly likely.

bugVerdicts.description: ahmed mobile-testing: Turbine StateFlow test asserts loading as the FIRST emission without consuming the replayed initial value, so the first awaitItem() returns the initial state, not the loading transition.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Lines 43-47 verified. A StateFlow replays its current value to every new collector. Turbine's Flow.test { } launches its collector with CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED, so on entering the block the collector immediately collects the StateFlow's current (initial) value into the channel before `onIntent(LoadItems)` runs. Thus the first `awaitItem()` returns the INITIAL state; `awaitItem().isLoading shouldBe true` asserts against it. For the common case where initial isLoading is false, the assertion fails; if initial isLoading happened to be true it 'passes' for the wrong reason. The correct pattern is to consume/skip the initial item (awaitItem()/skipItems(1)) before triggering the intent. The finding's secondary point is also sound: under StandardTestDispatcher, StateFlow conflation can drop the transient loading emission entirely (mockk coEvery returns without real suspension). The mechanism and fix are accurate. Severity minor is appropriate.

bugVerdicts.description: ahmed mobile-verification: uses @IdlingResource as a field annotation (no such annotation exists — IdlingResource is an interface) and references an undefined DisableAnimationsRule; the snippet is non-compiling / teaches a nonexistent API.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Lines 116-124 verified: `@IdlingResource val countingIdlingResource = CountingIdlingResource("api")` and `@get:Rule val disableAnimationsRule = DisableAnimationsRule()`. androidx.test.espresso.IdlingResource is an interface, not an annotation class; there is no @IdlingResource annotation in Espresso, so annotating a field with it does not compile and does nothing. The correct registration is IdlingRegistry.getInstance().register(countingIdlingResource). CountingIdlingResource("api") itself is a valid class, but the annotation-based 'registration' is fabricated. DisableAnimationsRule is not a standard AndroidX test API — it must be user-defined, so as written it is undefined. Both parts of the finding hold. Severity minor is fair (it's an illustrative-but-wrong snippet).

bugVerdicts.description: ahmed mobile-verification: presents CompositionLocalProvider(LocalInspectionMode provides true) as the fix for Compose flakiness whose stated causes are recomposition timing / state hoisting / animation interference — LocalInspectionMode addresses none of these.
bugVerdicts.reasoning: Lines 135-150 verified: the stated 'Common Flaky Causes' are 'Recomposition timing / State hoisting issues / Animation interference' and the 'Fix Strategies' block wraps content in CompositionLocalProvider(LocalInspectionMode provides true). LocalInspectionMode is a preview/inspection flag that some components read to render static placeholders (e.g., image loaders, maps) in previews; it does not control the test clock, recomposition scheduling, state hoisting, or animation frames. It cannot remedy any of the three listed causes. The correct levers (per rcosteira/android-testing lines 57-59) are mainClock.autoAdvance=false before setContent, advanceTimeByFrame(), and mainClock.advanceTimeUntil { }. It's a conceptually mismatched fix; while LocalInspectionMode can help with a different flake class (real image/network in previews), that is not what the file lists. Severity minor is appropriate.
